description: Role catalog for the seeded fleet. A scenario names a fixture ROLE; the runner (hack/fleet-kubeconfigs.sh) discovers the leased project's seeded clusters by label, matches each to a slot below, confirms every object in the role's `probes` list is present, and only then writes that role's kubeconfig. Nothing outside this file may address a seeded cluster or an eval project directly: each project carries its own trio, so a case written against one must run unchanged against all of them. Names, prefix and location are deliberately absent -- they are the Terraform's business and are read back off the discovered clusters. See README.md, 'Addressing a fixture by role'. One sanctioned exception, which discovers by these same labels and the trailing -<slot> name rule: hack/ci-eval-pr.sh section 3b reuses the slot-c cluster as the gpu-stress-test log-fixture subject -- it mutates nothing in-cluster, writes only project-level Cloud Logging entries that name the cluster, and falls back to a per-run cluster when slot c is absent, not RUNNING, or its default namespace is not empty. hack/fleet-fixture-state.py discovers nothing: it reads the slot's cluster name and location back out of the `.fleet-context` file the runner wrote, for the `cluster` state subjects below.
probe_syntax: Each probe is `<kind>/<name>` or `<kind>?<label-selector>`, read against the role's `namespace` when it has one. A role's namespace is probed implicitly. A probe is the runner's promise that the object was THERE before the agent ran, and it is the only thing that entitles a check to call the same object's later absence a violation rather than an environment that was never ready -- so every subject a task.yaml asserts on must appear here, which bench/tests/test_fleet_verifier.py enforces in both directions. A role with an empty list confirms nothing, and its checks can never blame the run for an absence.
state_syntax: Presence is not state (#1278: every probe passed while payments-api sat Pending on 30 projects). Each `state` entry is one assertion about the DESIGNED observable state of a role whose probes passed, evaluated by hack/fleet-fixture-state.py after the runner publishes the role: `subject` is a probe-shaped `<kind>/<name>`, `<kind>?<label-selector>` or bare `<kind>?` (every object of that kind in the role's namespace), or the word `cluster` for the GKE cluster carrying the role, read with `clusters describe` on the name the runner recorded; `path` is a dotted field path with `[*]`, `[N]` or `[?(@.key=='value')]` steps; `op` is `eq`, `ge`, `any_eq`, `any_ge`, `none_eq` (each with a `value`), `absent` (no value, no objects or no values at the path), `after_now` (an RFC 3339 timestamp still ahead), or `minor_behind_channel_default` (cluster subject only: the minor is `value` behind the cluster's own release channel default); `why` says what the cases lose when it fails. A role whose fixture is present but fails any assertion is DRIFTED: scripts/verify_ci_pool_project.py fails the project, and the script writes `<role>.drift` beside the role's kubeconfig, one failed assertion per line with what was observed (#1544). The presubmit does not run this pass and never acts on a drift; a scheduled scan of every pool project from the CI health bot is the follow-up on #1550. A role with an empty list asserts nothing beyond presence.

cluster_slots.a: Every namespace-level defect, plus the idle and pinned node pools.
cluster_slots.b: Control plane held one minor behind the REGULAR channel default, plus the upgrade-readiness drain defects.
cluster_slots.c: The consistency outlier: no master authorized networks.

crashloop-workload.fixture: payments-api Deployment, deterministic OOMKilled crashloop, 64Mi memory limit

state.subject: pod?app=payments-api
state.why: OOMKilled evidence exists only after the first restart. A pod that is Pending, or on its first start after a node rebuild, has none yet; the retest sweep after #1278 saw this lag the node repair by about 40 minutes on one project, which is why the presubmit waits for it rather than reading once

state.subject: pod?app=payments-api
state.why: the noun every crashloop case's root cause must contain. A crashloop for any other reason (an image pull, an eviction) is a different fixture from the one the cases were written against

no-pdb-workload.fixture: checkout-gateway Deployment, two replicas, no PodDisruptionBudget in the namespace

state.subject: deployment/checkout-gateway
state.why: the fleet's one healthy workload: cluster-agent-healthy-workload-no-finding asks whether the agent invents a fault, which means something only while both replicas are Running and Ready. On 2026-09-07 they sat Pending and the case could not be read either way

state.subject: poddisruptionbudget?
state.why: the defect is the missing budget; a PodDisruptionBudget anyone adds to seeded-reliability heals it and the no-pdb finding disappears

hpa-saturated.fixture: inference-server HPA settles above pinned-inference-pool's capped capacity, leaving Pending replicas. Both halves are probed: the HPA declares the gap and cluster-agent-pending-replicas-capped-pool additionally asserts the Deployment's nodeSelector and CPU request, the two fields that would make the Pending replicas schedulable

state.subject: deployment/inference-server
state.why: one Ready pod is what the HPA averages CPU over; with none Ready there is no metric, the HPA never scales, and the surplus the audit must quantify never appears

state.subject: pod?app=inference-server
state.why: the standing Pending surplus is the live shortfall stockout-pinned-pool and cluster-agent-pending-replicas-capped-pool read. It exists only while the HPA's desired count exceeds what the one-node pinned-inference-pool can place; a second node, or an HPA that never scaled, removes the defect

rbac-overgrant.fixture: debug-binding ClusterRoleBinding granting cluster-admin to the seeded-security default ServiceAccount

state.subject: clusterrolebinding/debug-binding
state.why: the over-grant is the role, not the binding's existence; a binding re-pointed at a narrower ClusterRole is a remediated fixture the compliance SOP's check 2.4 no longer flags

state.subject: clusterrolebinding/debug-binding
state.why: the subject is the seeded-security default ServiceAccount; the security cases name that namespace in their expected finding

idle-nodepool.fixture: idle-batch-pool node pool running zero non-system pods, held empty by a NO_SCHEDULE taint

state.subject: node?cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool=idle-batch-pool
state.why: a pool whose node is NotReady is not idle, it is broken: the cost SOP's idle check reads allocatable capacity off a Ready node, and a node mid-rebuild reads as a pool with nothing to report

state.subject: node?cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool=idle-batch-pool
state.why: the taint is what holds the pool at zero non-system pods. Without it kube-scheduler's least-allocated scoring lands the other defect workloads here and the idle finding is false

version-laggard.fixture: control plane one minor behind the REGULAR channel default, held by a NO_MINOR_UPGRADES exclusion

state.subject: cluster
state.why: the upgrade SOP's master-behind check compares a cluster against its OWN channel's default; a cluster taken off the channel falls out of the comparison and the lag is invisible to the audit it was planted for

state.subject: cluster
state.why: the defect itself. GKE upgrading the master -- reconciles lapsing past the exclusion window, or the held minor reaching end of life -- heals it, and upgrades-lagging-master-probe going red on every pull request is otherwise the first anyone hears of it

state.subject: cluster
state.why: the exclusion is what stops channel enrollment from healing the lag; a broader scope would also freeze the patch upgrades that keep the defect exactly one minor behind rather than unpatched

state.subject: cluster
state.why: every reconcile re-stamps the window from now. An end time already in the past means reconciles have lapsed and the next daily maintenance window upgrades the master -- this catches it the day before the case does

drift-outlier.fixture: master authorized networks absent where both cohort peers have it on

state.subject: cluster
state.why: the outlier facet. Anyone enabling authorized networks on slot c gives the drift cohort a 3/3 agreement and consistency-authorized-networks-probe nothing to find

readiness-surge-blocked.fixture: no-surge-pool node pool with max_surge 0 and max_unavailable 1, so an upgrade takes its only node away rather than adding a replacement first

state.subject: node?cloud.google.com/gke-nodepool=no-surge-pool
state.why: The pool's upgrade settings are readable from the GKE API whether or not its node is up, but the pinned workload below can only be Running if the node is, and the finding these two fixtures exist for is the pair. A NotReady node makes the workload Pending for a reason that is not the fixture

state.subject: cluster
state.why: the defect itself, as far as clusters describe exposes it: the pool upgrades by taking its only node away. Raising maxSurge back to 1 heals the fixture while every probe still passes, which is what this assertion exists to catch. maxSurge = 0 is the other half and is deliberately not asserted yet -- whether the API emits the zero or omits it is unconfirmed against a live apply, and an assertion guessed wrong leaves the role permanently drifted

readiness-pinned-workload.fixture: pinned-batch-runner Deployment (one replica), nodeSelector seeded-role=no-surge, so its pod runs only on the pool that cannot surge and has nowhere to go when it drains

state.subject: pod?app=pinned-batch-runner
state.why: The defect is that these pods have nowhere else to go, which is only true while they are somewhere. Pods already Pending carry no information about what a drain would do to them

state.subject: deployment/pinned-batch-runner
state.why: the pin is the defect. Drop the selector and the pod schedules onto the default pool, where a drain of the no-surge pool costs it nothing -- the fixture is healed and every probe still passes

readiness-failclosed-webhook.fixture: seeded-fail-closed-gate ValidatingWebhookConfiguration: failurePolicy Fail with the API's maximum 30-second timeout, pointing at a Service that does not exist, confined by namespaceSelector to seeded-upgrade

state.subject: validatingwebhookconfiguration/seeded-fail-closed-gate
state.why: Fail-closed is the whole defect: the same webhook with failurePolicy Ignore stalls no drain, so a run that read it as Ignore would be asserting against an object that is no longer the fixture

state.subject: validatingwebhookconfiguration/seeded-fail-closed-gate
state.why: the second half of the defect. An omitted timeout is defaulted to 10 by the API server, so the long wait is only present while it is set explicitly, and a check that grades how long a drain can stall has nothing to read if someone drops it

readiness-drain-blocked.fixture: pinned-batch-runner PodDisruptionBudget with maxUnavailable 0, so no pod it matches may ever be evicted voluntarily and every node drain that touches one blocks indefinitely

state.subject: poddisruptionbudget/pinned-batch-runner
state.why: the defect as the API reports it. Widen maxUnavailable to 1 and this becomes 1 while the pod is healthy, so the assertion catches the one edit that heals the fixture -- which no probe would, since the budget still exists

state.subject: poddisruptionbudget/pinned-batch-runner
state.why: the half that separates the defect from an unhealthy workload. disruptionsAllowed is also 0 when nothing is running, which is not this fixture; requiring a healthy pod alongside it means the zero is the spec's doing. hpa-saturated pairs its assertion the same way
